stem: A request reaches the Kubernetes API server. Which stage decides whether the authenticated user is **allowed** to perform the requested verb on the resource?

options.text: Authentication, which checks client certificates or tokens
options.why: Authentication only establishes who the caller is, not what they may do.

options.text: Authorization, for example the RBAC authorizer
options.why: Authorization evaluates the user, verb and resource against policy such as RBAC.

options.text: Mutating admission, which can rewrite the incoming object
options.why: Admission runs after authorization and inspects or changes the object itself.

options.text: Validation by etcd before the object is written to disk
options.why: etcd stores data; it makes no access decisions for API clients.

explanation: Every API request passes authentication (who are you?), then authorization (may you do this verb on this resource?), then admission control (is this particular object acceptable, possibly after mutation?). RBAC is the usual authorizer.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API

stem: An RBAC Role can contain a rule that explicitly **denies** `delete` on Pods, overriding permissions granted by another RoleBinding.

options.text: True
options.why: RBAC has no deny rules, so this statement is wrong.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: RBAC permissions are purely additive; there is no way to write a deny rule.

explanation: RBAC rules only grant access. A subject's effective permissions are the union of every Role and ClusterRole bound to it, so the only way to remove access is to remove or change a binding. Deny-style controls need an admission policy instead.

stem: A platform team wants to let a monitoring group `get` and `list` **Nodes**. Which RBAC objects grant that?

options.text: A Role in `kube-system` bound with a RoleBinding in `kube-system`
options.why: A Role is namespaced and cannot grant access to cluster-scoped objects like Nodes.

options.text: A ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding in the `default` namespace
options.why: A RoleBinding scopes the ClusterRole to one namespace, so cluster-scoped Nodes are not covered.

options.text: A ClusterRole bound with a ClusterRoleBinding
options.why: Cluster-scoped resources such as Nodes can only be granted cluster-wide.

options.text: A ServiceAccount annotated with the Node resource names
options.why: Annotations on a ServiceAccount grant nothing; RBAC objects do.

explanation: Nodes are cluster-scoped. Roles and RoleBindings live in a namespace and can only grant namespaced resources, so access to Nodes needs a ClusterRole plus a ClusterRoleBinding.

stem: A Pod manifest does not set `serviceAccountName`. Which ServiceAccount does the Pod run as?

options.text: The `default` ServiceAccount of the Pod's namespace
options.why: Every namespace gets a `default` ServiceAccount, and Pods use it unless told otherwise.

options.text: No ServiceAccount, so the Pod cannot call the API at all
options.why: Pods always have a ServiceAccount; the default one is assigned automatically.

options.text: The `default` ServiceAccount in the `kube-system` namespace
options.why: ServiceAccounts are namespaced; a Pod uses one from its own namespace.

options.text: The identity of the user who ran `kubectl apply`
options.why: Pods never inherit the identity of whoever created them.

explanation: Each namespace automatically gets a ServiceAccount called `default`. A Pod that omits `serviceAccountName` runs as that account, and by default its token is mounted into the Pod.

stem: The Pod Security Standards define three profiles: privileged, baseline, and a third, most locked-down profile. Type the name of that third profile.
explanation: The Pod Security Standards are `privileged` (unrestricted), `baseline` (blocks known privilege escalations such as hostPath and privileged containers) and `restricted` (current hardening best practice: non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, a seccomp profile set).

stem: A namespace contains Pods, and no NetworkPolicy selects any of them. What traffic can reach those Pods?

options.text: Only traffic from Pods in the same namespace
options.why: There is no implicit namespace isolation without a policy.

options.text: No traffic, because Pods are isolated until a policy allows it
options.why: Isolation only starts once a policy selects the Pod.

options.text: All traffic, because Pods are non-isolated by default
options.why: A Pod becomes isolated for a direction only when some policy selects it.

options.text: Only traffic that passes through a Service
options.why: Pod-to-Pod traffic by IP is allowed too unless a policy says otherwise.

explanation: By default Pods are non-isolated and accept traffic from any source. A Pod becomes isolated for ingress or egress only when at least one NetworkPolicy selects it for that direction; from then on, only traffic some policy allows gets through.

stem: Match each container `securityContext` setting with its effect.

options.text: The container cannot start if its image would run as UID 0
Writes to the container's root filesystem fail
A process cannot gain more privileges than its parent, for example via setuid binaries
The container starts with no Linux capabilities

explanation: `runAsNonRoot` makes the kubelet refuse to start a container that would run as root. `readOnlyRootFilesystem` mounts the image filesystem read-only. `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` sets the no_new_privs flag, so setuid binaries cannot raise privileges. Dropping ALL capabilities removes even the default set the runtime grants.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

stem: Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted in etcd by default, so anyone with direct read access to etcd still cannot see their values.

options.text: True
options.why: By default Secret data is stored unencrypted in etcd, so this is wrong.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: without an encryption configuration on the API server, Secret data is stored unencrypted (only base64-encoded) in etcd.

explanation: The API server stores Secrets unencrypted in etcd unless you configure encryption at rest with an EncryptionConfiguration (for example the KMS v2 provider). Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, so anyone who can read etcd or its backups can read the values.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Encrypting Confidential Data at Rest

stem:
You create this binding in namespace `payments`. What can members of group `auditors` do?

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: auditors-view
  namespace: payments
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view
subjects:
- kind: Group
  name: auditors
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

options.text: Read most objects in every namespace, since `view` is a ClusterRole
options.why: A ClusterRole referenced from a RoleBinding only grants access inside that binding's namespace.

options.text: Read most objects in `payments` only
options.why: A RoleBinding scopes the referenced ClusterRole to its own namespace.

options.text: Nothing, because a RoleBinding cannot reference a ClusterRole
options.why: Referencing a ClusterRole from a RoleBinding is supported and common.

options.text: Read everything in `payments`, including Secrets
options.why: The built-in `view` role deliberately excludes Secrets.

explanation: A RoleBinding may reference a ClusterRole; the permissions then apply only within the RoleBinding's namespace. This lets you define a role once and reuse it per namespace. The built-in `view` ClusterRole allows reading most namespaced objects but not Secrets.

stem: In namespace `dev`, which permissions let a user end up reading the **contents** of Secrets in `dev`? (Choose three.)

options.text: `get` on `secrets`
options.why: Getting a Secret returns its data.

options.text: `list` on `secrets`
options.why: A list response includes every Secret's data, not just the names.

options.text: `create` on `pods`
options.why: A new Pod can mount any Secret in its namespace and print it.

options.text: `get` on `configmaps`
options.why: ConfigMaps are separate objects and give no access to Secrets.

options.text: `get` on `pods/log` for existing Pods
options.why: Reading logs exposes only what existing apps chose to log.

options.text: `list` on `serviceaccounts`
options.why: Listing ServiceAccounts shows names, not Secret values.

explanation: Both `get` and `list` on Secrets return the data (`list` and `watch` reveal contents, which is an easy one to miss). Permission to create Pods is indirect access: the Pod can mount any Secret in the namespace as a volume or env var and then expose it. The RBAC docs warn about this escalation path.

stem: An admin runs `kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n dev --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:builder`. What does this check, and what does the admin need for it to work?

options.text: Whether the admin personally can delete pods; it only needs `delete` on pods itself
options.why: With `--as`, the check is for the impersonated identity, not the admin.

options.text: Whether `builder` may delete pods in `dev`; the admin needs `impersonate`
options.why: Impersonation asks the authorizer about another identity and itself requires the `impersonate` verb.

options.text: Whether `builder` has deleted pods recently; it reads the audit log
options.why: can-i asks the authorizer a question; it does not read audit history.

options.text: Whether `builder`'s token is still valid; it needs `get secrets`
options.why: can-i checks authorization, not token validity.

explanation: `kubectl auth can-i` asks the API server, via a SelfSubjectAccessReview, whether an action would be allowed. With `--as`, kubectl impersonates the named user or ServiceAccount, which the caller can only do if they hold the `impersonate` verb on users, groups or serviceaccounts.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Authorization Overview (Checking API access)

stem: A Deployment's Pods never call the Kubernetes API. What does setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` in the Pod spec change?

options.text: The Pod is rejected unless it also sets `serviceAccountName` to a non-default account
options.why: The setting is valid on its own and does not require a named account.

options.text: The ServiceAccount is deleted when the Pod starts
options.why: It only affects what is mounted into this Pod.

options.text: No API token is mounted, so a compromised container has no credential to steal
options.why: Without the projected token there is nothing to use against the API server.

options.text: The Pod gets an anonymous token with read-only access instead
options.why: No replacement token is mounted at all.

explanation: By default the kubelet projects a ServiceAccount token into every Pod. If the app never talks to the API server, setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` (on the Pod or the ServiceAccount) removes that credential, which limits what an attacker who compromises the container can do.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Configure Service Accounts for Pods

stem: Namespace `legacy` has only this label: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted`. A user creates a Pod that runs as root. What happens?

options.text: The Pod is rejected with a Forbidden error
options.why: Only the `enforce` mode rejects Pods.

options.text: The Pod is admitted, and the violation is recorded in the audit log
options.why: The `audit` mode only adds an audit annotation; it never blocks.

options.text: The Pod is admitted and kubectl prints a warning
options.why: Client warnings come from the `warn` mode, which isn't set here.

options.text: The Pod is mutated by admission so that it runs as a non-root user instead
options.why: Pod Security Admission validates; it never mutates Pods.

explanation: Pod Security Admission has three independent modes per namespace: `enforce` rejects violating Pods, `audit` records violations as audit-log annotations, and `warn` returns a warning to the client. With only `audit` set, the Pod is created normally and the violation shows up in the audit log.

stem:
Namespace `apps` enforces the `restricted` Pod Security Standard. This Pod is rejected. Which setting must change for it to be admitted?

```yaml
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: registry.example.com/api@sha256:4f1c...
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

options.text: Add `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` to the container
options.why: A read-only root filesystem is good practice, but `restricted` does not require it.

options.text: Add `capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }` to the container
options.why: `restricted` requires every container to drop ALL capabilities.

options.text: Set `runAsUser: 1000` explicitly on the Pod
options.why: `runAsNonRoot: true` already satisfies the non-root requirement.

options.text: Replace `RuntimeDefault` with `Unconfined` for compatibility
options.why: `Unconfined` is forbidden by the restricted profile.

explanation: The `restricted` profile requires `runAsNonRoot: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, a seccomp profile of `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`, and containers that drop `ALL` capabilities (only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` may be added back). This Pod is missing the capability drop.

stem:
After applying this policy in namespace `shop`, the app can no longer resolve `orders.shop.svc.cluster.local`. Why?

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-to-db
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels: { app: postgres }
    ports:
    - port: 5432
```

options.text: Once any NetworkPolicy exists in a namespace, all DNS lookups there are blocked cluster-wide
options.why: Only Pods selected by a policy are affected, and only in the listed directions.

options.text: Web Pods are now egress-isolated, and no rule allows port 53 to cluster DNS
options.why: An egress allow-list must explicitly include DNS to kube-dns in kube-system.

options.text: `policyTypes` must list both Ingress and Egress or DNS breaks
options.why: Listing Egress alone is valid; the problem is the missing DNS rule.

options.text: Port 5432 conflicts with the DNS port range
options.why: Port numbers in a rule don't interfere with other ports; they just aren't allowed.

explanation: Once a policy selects the web Pods for egress, only the listed destinations are allowed. DNS queries go to the CoreDNS Pods in `kube-system` on port 53 (UDP and TCP), so a rule allowing that traffic has to be added, typically using a namespaceSelector for kube-system and the DNS Pods' labels.

stem: A developer needs to `kubectl exec` into Pods in namespace `dev`. In an RBAC rule, besides `get` on `pods`, which resource must be granted the `create` verb? Type the resource name as it appears in the rule.
explanation: `kubectl exec` opens a connection to the `exec` subresource of a Pod, which RBAC writes as `pods/exec`. Recent kubectl versions use the `create` verb for it (older ones used `get`), so a rule usually grants `create` and `get` on `pods/exec`. Subresources like `pods/log` and `pods/exec` must be granted separately from `pods`.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization (Referring to resources)

stem: How do the ServiceAccount tokens that the kubelet projects into Pods today differ from the legacy tokens stored in Secrets?

options.text: Projected tokens never expire, so they need no rotation
options.why: Projected tokens are short-lived and rotated by the kubelet.

options.text: Legacy tokens are bound to the Pod and invalidated when it is deleted
options.why: That describes the projected tokens, not the legacy Secret-based ones.

options.text: Projected tokens are time-limited and bound to the Pod and an audience
options.why: They are minted via the TokenRequest API with an expiry, audience and object binding.

options.text: Projected tokens are only valid for clients that run outside the cluster network
options.why: They are meant for workloads in the Pod, typically to call the API server.

explanation: Pods now receive tokens from the TokenRequest API through a projected volume. These tokens expire (the kubelet refreshes them), carry an audience, and are bound to the Pod, so they stop working once the Pod is deleted. Legacy tokens stored in Secrets never expire, which is why Kubernetes stopped auto-creating them.

stem: If the cluster's network plugin does not implement NetworkPolicy, creating NetworkPolicy objects still blocks the traffic they deny.

options.text: True
options.why: NetworkPolicy needs an enforcing plugin, so this is wrong.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the API server stores the objects, but nothing enforces them without a supporting network plugin.

explanation: NetworkPolicy is implemented by the network plugin (for example Calico or Cilium). On a cluster whose plugin doesn't support it, the API accepts the objects but they have no effect, which can give a false sense of security.

stem: A team deploys `image: registry.example.com/api:1.4` in production. Which risk does pinning the image by digest (`api@sha256:...`) remove?

options.text: The tag being repointed, so nodes may run content you never reviewed
options.why: A digest names exact content, so it cannot change underneath you.

options.text: The need to scan images for known vulnerabilities
options.why: A pinned image can still contain vulnerabilities and needs scanning.

options.text: Pulling from a private registry without configuring any imagePullSecrets at all
options.why: Digests don't change how registry authentication works.

options.text: Containers running as root inside the image
options.why: Which user runs is set by the image and securityContext, not the reference.

explanation: Tags are mutable pointers: someone can push new content under `1.4`, and different nodes may pull different images. A digest is the hash of the image manifest, so it always resolves to the same content, which supports reproducible deployments and signature verification.

stem:
Which statement about these two ingress rules is correct?

```yaml
# Policy X
ingress:
- from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { team: a }
    podSelector:
      matchLabels: { role: client }
---
# Policy Y
ingress:
- from:
  - namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { team: a }
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels: { role: client }
```

options.text: X and Y are equivalent; the extra dash in Y only changes how the YAML is formatted, not the rules
options.why: The dash creates a separate list element, which changes the meaning.

options.text: X: `role: client` Pods in `team: a` namespaces. Y: any Pod in those namespaces, or local `role: client` Pods
options.why: One element combines selectors with AND; two elements are ORed.

options.text: X allows any Pod in `team: a` namespaces, while Y allows only `role: client` Pods across every namespace
options.why: This reverses the AND and OR semantics of the two forms.

options.text: Y is invalid: a `from` list may only contain one peer, so the API server rejects the second element
options.why: A `from` list can hold several peers, which are ORed together.

explanation: Within one `from` element, `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` are combined with AND. Separate elements are ORed, and a bare `podSelector` element means Pods in the policy's own namespace. The NetworkPolicy docs call out this single-dash difference as a common source of mistakes.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Network Policies (Behavior of to and from selectors)

stem: A CI ServiceAccount in namespace `build` can `create` Pods but has no permission on Secrets. A highly privileged ServiceAccount `deployer` also lives in `build`. What can an attacker with the CI token do?

options.text: Nothing beyond creating Pods, since Secret access was never granted
options.why: Pods can run as other ServiceAccounts in the namespace.

options.text: Create a Pod with `serviceAccountName: deployer` and use its mounted token
options.why: Creating Pods lets you run as any ServiceAccount in that namespace.

options.text: Read Secrets only if the `build` namespace has no Pod Security labels set on it
options.why: Pod Security Admission doesn't govern which ServiceAccount a Pod uses.

options.text: Escalate only if `deployer` has a ClusterRoleBinding
options.why: Namespace-scoped permissions of `deployer` are already enough to abuse.

explanation: Permission to create Pods (or workloads that create Pods) in a namespace implies the ability to run as any ServiceAccount there and to mount any Secret there. The RBAC good-practice guide lists this as an escalation path. Keep high-privilege ServiceAccounts in namespaces where few people can create Pods.

stem: Which RBAC permissions are explicitly called out as allowing **privilege escalation** if granted carelessly? (Choose three.)

options.text: `bind` on roles or clusterroles
options.why: It lets a user bind roles whose permissions they don't hold.

options.text: `escalate` on roles or clusterroles
options.why: It lets a user create or edit roles with permissions they don't hold.

options.text: `impersonate` on users, groups or serviceaccounts
options.why: It lets a user act as a more privileged identity.

options.text: `get` on `pods`
options.why: Reading Pod specs does not grant any new permissions.

options.text: `list` on `events`
options.why: Events reveal activity but give no way to gain rights.

options.text: `watch` on `configmaps`
options.why: ConfigMaps hold non-secret config and grant no new access.

explanation: RBAC normally stops users from granting permissions they don't have. The `escalate` verb lifts that check for creating or updating Roles, and the `bind` verb lifts it for creating bindings to Roles. `impersonate` lets a user act as any other identity, including more privileged ones. These three verbs should be granted to very few subjects.

stem: A Role in namespace `dev` has `apiGroups: ["*"]`, `resources: ["*"]`, `verbs: ["*"]`, bound to a developer group. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It grants full cluster-admin, including Nodes and every other namespace in the cluster
options.why: A Role can never grant access outside its namespace or to cluster-scoped objects.

options.text: It grants everything in `dev`, including Secrets and resource types added later
options.why: Wildcards match every namespaced resource now and in the future.

options.text: It is rejected, because Roles may not use wildcards
options.why: Wildcards are allowed in rules; they are just risky.

options.text: It grants all verbs except `delete`, which must be listed explicitly
options.why: The `*` verb includes delete and every other verb.

explanation: Wildcards in a Role match every namespaced resource in that namespace, including Secrets and any CRD types installed later, and every verb. The RBAC good-practice guide advises against them because new resources become accessible automatically. A Role can still never reach cluster-scoped resources or other namespaces.

stem: An employee who left still has a valid client certificate with organization `O=system:masters`. You delete every RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding naming them. What can they still do?

options.text: Nothing, because RBAC no longer grants them anything
options.why: Members of `system:masters` don't depend on RBAC bindings.

options.text: Everything: `system:masters` skips authorization until the certificate expires
options.why: This group is a superuser group that skips authorization checks.

options.text: Read-only access through the built-in `view` role
options.why: There is no automatic fallback to `view` for this group.

options.text: Only the actions that the audit policy logs as warnings, since those are still allowed
options.why: Audit logging records actions but doesn't restrict them.

explanation: The `system:masters` group bypasses authorization entirely, so removing bindings has no effect. Client certificates can't be revoked individually by Kubernetes, so the access lasts until the certificate expires or the cluster CA is rotated. Avoid issuing `system:masters` certificates to people.

stem: You want the API server itself to reject any Pod whose image is not from `registry.example.com`, with no extra webhook to run. You write a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with a CEL expression. What else is required before it takes effect?

options.text: Nothing; a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy applies as soon as it is created
options.why: A policy does nothing until something binds it to resources.

options.text: A ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding that selects the target resources
options.why: The binding attaches the policy and sets enforcement actions like Deny.

options.text: A Pod Security Admission label on every namespace
options.why: Pod Security Admission is a separate mechanism with fixed profiles.

options.text: An OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate for the CEL rule
options.why: CEL policies run in-process; no Gatekeeper is needed.

explanation: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (GA in Kubernetes 1.30) evaluates CEL expressions inside the API server. A policy defines the checks; a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding decides which resources and namespaces it applies to and which validation actions (Deny, Warn, Audit) to take.

stem: Namespace `web` has the label `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`. A Deployment with a privileged container is applied: kubectl reports success, but no Pods appear. Why?

options.text: Pod Security Admission rejected the Deployment, but kubectl hides the error
options.why: The Deployment object itself was created successfully.

options.text: `enforce` applies to Pods, so the ReplicaSet's Pod creations are rejected
options.why: Enforcement checks Pod objects; the rejection shows up as events on the ReplicaSet.

options.text: The scheduler skips privileged Pods in restricted namespaces
options.why: The Pods are never created, so the scheduler never sees them.

options.text: Privileged Pods need a separate PodSecurityPolicy to be created
options.why: PodSecurityPolicy was removed in Kubernetes 1.25.

explanation: In `enforce` mode, Pod Security Admission only evaluates Pod objects. The Deployment and ReplicaSet are created, but each Pod creation by the ReplicaSet controller is rejected, which appears as FailedCreate events on the ReplicaSet. The `warn` and `audit` modes also check workload resources, which is why adding a `warn` label surfaces the problem at apply time.

stem: Match each policy mechanism with how it works.

options.text: Built-in admission plugin that applies the three fixed Pod Security Standards via namespace labels
CEL expressions evaluated inside the API server, attached with a binding
External validating webhook that evaluates Rego policies defined through ConstraintTemplates
Admission webhook whose policies are written as Kubernetes YAML and can validate, mutate and generate resources

explanation: Pod Security Admission is built in but only knows the fixed profiles. ValidatingAdmissionPolicy runs custom CEL checks in-process. Gatekeeper and Kyverno are webhook-based policy engines: Gatekeeper uses Rego via ConstraintTemplates, while Kyverno uses YAML policies and can also mutate and generate resources.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Admission Control; Validating Admission Policy

stem: Which Pod spec settings effectively give a container root-level access to the node it runs on? (Choose three.)

options.text: `privileged: true` on a container
options.why: Privileged containers get all capabilities and access to host devices.

options.text: A `hostPath` volume mounting `/` from the node
options.why: Writing to the node filesystem lets you change host binaries or configuration.

options.text: `hostPID: true` combined with running as root
options.why: Sharing the host PID namespace lets a root process inspect and enter host processes.

options.text: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: false`
options.why: A writable container filesystem is the default and stays inside the container.

options.text: `runAsUser: 1000` with all capabilities dropped
options.why: This is a hardened, unprivileged configuration.

options.text: Adding only the `NET_BIND_SERVICE` capability
options.why: It only allows binding to ports below 1024.

explanation: Privileged containers, writable hostPath mounts of sensitive host paths, and host namespaces (hostPID, hostNetwork, hostIPC) all break the isolation between container and node. The `baseline` Pod Security Standard forbids all of them.

stem: An attacker compromises one worker node and steals its kubelet credentials (user `system:node:worker-2`, group `system:nodes`). The cluster uses the Node authorizer and the NodeRestriction admission plugin. What can those credentials still do?

options.text: Modify any Node object in the cluster, including removing taints from other nodes
options.why: NodeRestriction lets a kubelet modify only its own Node object, and not its taints.

options.text: Read and update every Pod in every namespace, because kubelets manage all workloads cluster-wide
options.why: A kubelet is limited to Pod objects bound to its own node.

options.text: Modify its own Node object and only the Pods bound to worker-2
options.why: The plugin confines a kubelet's writes to its own Node and the Pods scheduled on it.

options.text: Delete its own Node object to hide from the control plane
options.why: NodeRestriction explicitly prevents kubelets from deleting their own Node object.

explanation: The NodeRestriction admission plugin limits the Node and Pod objects a kubelet can modify. Kubelets that authenticate in the `system:nodes` group with a `system:node:<nodeName>` username may only modify their own Node object and Pods bound to their node. They also can't update or remove taints on their Node, can't delete their Node object, and are restricted in setting labels under the kubernetes.io prefixes. Combined with the Node authorizer, this limits the blast radius of one compromised node.

stem: A security scan finds that a node's kubelet port 10250 answers unauthenticated requests. What is the risk, and what is the right fix?

options.text: Only node metrics leak, so restricting the read-only port 10255 on the node fixes it
options.why: The authenticated port 10250 exposes far more than metrics.

options.text: Callers can exec into Pods; disable anonymous auth and use Webhook authorization
options.why: The kubelet API can run commands in containers, so it must authenticate and authorize callers.

options.text: Nothing serious, because the kubelet API is read-only
options.why: The kubelet API includes exec, attach and port-forward endpoints.

options.text: A NetworkPolicy in kube-system is enough to close it
options.why: NetworkPolicies select Pods, not the kubelet process on the host.

explanation: The kubelet's HTTPS API (port 10250) can list Pods and run commands inside containers. If anonymous requests are allowed and authorization is AlwaysAllow, anyone who can reach the port controls the node's workloads. Disable anonymous auth, enable Webhook authorization so the API server decides, and restrict network access to the port.

stem: Which statements about NetworkPolicy semantics are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: Policies are additive; traffic allowed by any selecting policy is allowed
options.why: There is no ordering or deny rule; allowed sets are unioned.

options.text: Ingress and egress isolation are independent of each other
options.why: A Pod can be isolated for egress while ingress stays open, and vice versa.

options.text: Reply traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically
options.why: Policies act on connections, so responses don't need their own rule.

options.text: A later policy can override and deny traffic another policy allows
options.why: NetworkPolicy has no deny rules or precedence.

options.text: Selecting a Pod in one namespace isolates every Pod in that namespace
options.why: Only Pods matched by the policy's podSelector become isolated.

options.text: An empty `podSelector: {}` selects no Pods
options.why: An empty selector selects every Pod in the namespace.

explanation: NetworkPolicies are allow-lists. Each direction is isolated separately, only for Pods a policy selects, and the allowed traffic is the union of all applicable policies. They are connection-oriented, so return traffic is implicitly allowed. `podSelector: {}` selects all Pods in the namespace, which is the usual way to write a default-deny policy.

stem: Which built-in user-facing ClusterRole lets a subject read most objects in a namespace but deliberately excludes Secrets? Type its name.
explanation: Kubernetes ships the user-facing ClusterRoles `cluster-admin`, `admin`, `edit` and `view`. `view` allows read-only access to most objects but not Secrets, because reading Secrets (and ServiceAccount tokens) would allow escalation. `edit` and `admin` do allow access to Secrets.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization (User-facing roles)

stem: You want to move an existing namespace to the `restricted` Pod Security Standard without breaking running workloads. Put the steps in a safe order.

options.text: Label the namespace with `warn` and `audit` set to `restricted`
Review the warnings and audit annotations for violating workloads
Fix the workloads' securityContext settings and roll them out
Add `enforce: restricted` to the namespace labels

explanation: Pod Security Admission's `warn` and `audit` modes surface violations without blocking anything, including on workload resources. After fixing the reported workloads, switching on `enforce` won't reject the next round of Pod creations. A server-side dry run of the label change also lists violating Pods.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Migrate from PodSecurityPolicy / Enforce Pod Security Standards

stem:
This RoleBinding exists in namespace `dev`. Who gets the `edit` permissions?

```yaml
subjects:
- kind: Group
  name: system:serviceaccounts:dev
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

options.text: Only the `default` ServiceAccount in `dev`
options.why: The group covers every ServiceAccount in the namespace, not just `default`.

options.text: Every ServiceAccount in `dev`, including ones created later
options.why: The `system:serviceaccounts:<ns>` group contains all ServiceAccounts in that namespace.

options.text: Every ServiceAccount in the cluster
options.why: That would be the `system:serviceaccounts` group without the namespace suffix.

options.text: No one, because RBAC does not accept Groups as subjects of a RoleBinding
options.why: Groups are valid subjects, and ServiceAccounts belong to built-in groups.

explanation: Every ServiceAccount is in the groups `system:serviceaccounts` and `system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>`. Binding the namespaced group grants the role to all current and future ServiceAccounts there, so any Pod in `dev` gets `edit`, including access to Secrets. That is usually far broader than intended.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization (Referring to subjects)

stem: A developer may `patch` Deployments in namespace `prod` but has no rights on Pods or Secrets. Why does a security review flag this as dangerous?

options.text: Patching a Deployment lets them read Secret values through the Deployment object itself
options.why: The Deployment object doesn't contain Secret data.

options.text: They can edit the Pod template to use any ServiceAccount and mount any Secret
options.why: The controller creates Pods from whatever template they write.

options.text: It isn't dangerous: without `create pods` no new Pods can appear
options.why: The ReplicaSet controller creates Pods with its own permissions.

options.text: They can bind ClusterRoles by adding annotations to the Deployment
options.why: Annotations on a Deployment grant no RBAC permissions.

explanation: Workload controllers create Pods using their own permissions, from the template you supply. Anyone who can create or modify Deployments, ReplicaSets, StatefulSets, Jobs or CronJobs can effectively run arbitrary Pods, including choosing any ServiceAccount and mounting any Secret in the namespace. Treat workload write access like Pod creation access.
reference: Kubernetes docs: RBAC Good Practices (Workload creation)

stem: Several customers share one cluster, each in its own namespace. Which controls together give meaningful isolation between tenants? (Choose three.)

options.text: Enforcing the `restricted` Pod Security Standard on tenant namespaces
options.why: It stops tenants from running privileged or host-level Pods that escape to the node.

options.text: Default-deny NetworkPolicies plus explicit allows
options.why: Without them any Pod can reach any other tenant's Pods.

options.text: Namespace-scoped RBAC with no cluster-wide bindings for tenants
options.why: Tenants should only be granted rights inside their own namespace.

options.text: Separate namespaces alone, since they are hard security boundaries
options.why: Namespaces scope names and policies but don't isolate nodes or networks.

options.text: Unique Service names per tenant to avoid DNS collisions
options.why: Naming hygiene doesn't restrict access between tenants.

options.text: Giving each tenant a separate kubeconfig context
options.why: A context is client-side configuration with no security effect.

explanation: Namespaces are a soft boundary. Real multi-tenancy layers RBAC scoped to each namespace, Pod Security to block node-level escape, NetworkPolicies for traffic, resource quotas, and for hostile tenants node isolation or sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata.

stem: You install a CRD and want users with the built-in `view` role to be able to read the new resources. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a ClusterRole for the CRD labelled `rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view: "true"`
options.why: The built-in `view` role aggregates rules from ClusterRoles carrying this label.

options.text: Existing bindings to `view` pick up the new rules without being changed
options.why: Aggregation updates the `view` role itself, so every binding to it benefits.

options.text: You must edit the `view` ClusterRole directly and add the CRD resources
options.why: Direct edits are overwritten, because the aggregation controller manages its rules.

options.text: CRDs are automatically included in `view` when they are installed
options.why: New resources are only added when a labelled ClusterRole exists.

options.text: You must create a separate RoleBinding in every namespace
options.why: Bindings stay as they are; only the role's rules change.

explanation: The default `view`, `edit` and `admin` ClusterRoles are aggregated: a controller fills their rules from ClusterRoles carrying labels such as `rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view: "true"`. Adding a labelled ClusterRole for a CRD extends every existing binding, and manual edits to the aggregated role are overwritten.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization (Aggregated ClusterRoles)

stem: A NetworkPolicy uses `ipBlock: { cidr: 203.0.113.0/24 }` to allow a partner's clients into a Service exposed by a cloud load balancer, but legitimate partner traffic is still dropped. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: ipBlock only matches IPv6 addresses
options.why: ipBlock accepts both IPv4 and IPv6 CIDRs.

options.text: Source NAT on the load-balancer path, so Pods never see the client IP
options.why: Source NAT on the path means the client IP may never reach the Pod.

options.text: ipBlock rules apply only to egress, never ingress
options.why: ipBlock is valid in both ingress `from` and egress `to` rules.

options.text: NetworkPolicies cannot select Pods that sit behind a Service of type LoadBalancer
options.why: Policies select Pods by label, whether or not a Service fronts them.

explanation: ipBlock matches the source address the Pod actually sees. Traffic through load balancers or NodePorts may be source-NATed, so the original client IP is gone, and the docs warn that ipBlock behaviour for such traffic is implementation-defined. `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` or the load balancer's own allow-lists are more reliable.

stem: Pods on cloud nodes can reach the instance metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254`. Why do hardening guides recommend blocking that from Pods and using workload identity instead?

options.text: The endpoint slows down DNS resolution for every Pod
options.why: Metadata access has nothing to do with DNS performance.

options.text: Any Pod could use the node's cloud credentials and all of its permissions
options.why: Workload identity maps each ServiceAccount to its own narrowly scoped cloud role.

options.text: Kubernetes forbids Pods from opening link-local addresses
options.why: Link-local traffic is allowed unless you block it.

options.text: Metadata responses are often stale, so apps end up using the wrong credentials
options.why: The credentials are valid; the risk is that they are too powerful.

explanation: The node's instance role is shared by every Pod scheduled there. Workload identity schemes such as IRSA, GKE Workload Identity or Azure Workload Identity exchange a projected ServiceAccount token with a cloud-specific audience for credentials scoped to that one workload, and metadata access is blocked with network policy or provider settings.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Service Accounts (Bound service account tokens)

stem: Your audit policy logs everything at the `RequestResponse` level. A security review says this leaks credentials. What is the recommended change?

options.text: Switch every resource to `None` to stop collecting audit data
options.why: Turning off auditing removes visibility instead of fixing the leak.

options.text: Log Secrets, ConfigMaps and token requests at `Metadata` level
options.why: `Metadata` records who did what without capturing request or response bodies.

options.text: Keep `RequestResponse`, but base64-encode the audit log file on the disk
options.why: Encoding doesn't protect the values.

options.text: Log Secrets at the `Request` level only
options.why: The `Request` level still records the body of create and update calls.

explanation: Audit levels are `None`, `Metadata`, `Request` and `RequestResponse`. At `Request` and above, the bodies of Secret writes and reads end up in the log. The docs' example policy logs Secrets, ConfigMaps and TokenReviews only at `Metadata`, and keeps request bodies for less sensitive resources.

stem: Which controls ensure at admission time that only images built by your pipeline can run? (Choose two.)

options.text: An admission policy that verifies image signatures, for example Kyverno verifyImages or Sigstore policy-controller
options.why: Signature checks prove the image came from your signing identity.

options.text: An admission policy that rejects images not referenced by digest
options.why: Digests make the verified content exactly what runs.

options.text: Setting `imagePullPolicy: Always` on every container
options.why: It only forces a fresh pull of whatever the tag points to.

options.text: Scanning images for CVEs in CI before pushing them
options.why: Scanning is useful, but nothing at admission stops unscanned images.

options.text: Using a private registry that requires imagePullSecrets
options.why: Credentials don't prove who built the image.

explanation: Supply-chain controls need enforcement in the cluster. Admission policies can verify a signature (and optionally attestations such as SBOMs or provenance) against your signing identity, and require digest references so the verified content is what actually runs. Pull policies, registries and CI scans don't stop an unverified image at deploy time.

stem:
What happens when you apply this container spec?

```yaml
securityContext:
  privileged: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

options.text: The container runs privileged, and the escalation setting is silently ignored
options.why: The combination is rejected rather than partly applied.

options.text: The API server rejects it, because privileged containers can always escalate
options.why: Validation forbids allowPrivilegeEscalation false together with privileged true.

options.text: The container runs unprivileged, because the stricter setting wins
options.why: Kubernetes doesn't pick one; it rejects the conflict.

options.text: The kubelet starts it and logs a warning event about the conflict
options.why: The object fails API validation before any kubelet sees it.

explanation: A privileged container always has every capability, so it can always escalate. API validation therefore rejects `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` combined with `privileged: true`, and likewise combined with adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`. The docs note that allowPrivilegeEscalation is always true when the container is privileged or has CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

stem: Jane authenticates with a client certificate whose subject is `CN=jane, O=dev, O=qa`. To cut her access to the `payments` namespace, an admin deletes the RoleBinding whose subject is `User: jane`. Jane can still list Secrets in `payments`. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: A RoleBinding grants access to Group dev or qa, which her certificate still carries
options.why: Each O field becomes a group, so bindings to those groups still apply.

options.text: RBAC caches decisions for the lifetime of the client certificate, so the change applies on renewal
options.why: RBAC changes take effect on new requests; there is no per-certificate decision cache.

options.text: Usernames come from the O field, so the deleted binding never matched her identity
options.why: The CN is the username; the O fields become group memberships.

options.text: Client-certificate users bypass RBAC entirely and are limited only by the admission controllers that run
options.why: Certificate users are authorized by RBAC like any other user; only special groups such as system:masters bypass it.

explanation: With X.509 client certificate authentication, the subject's common name becomes the username and each organization (O) field becomes a group the user belongs to. Removing a binding for `User: jane` does nothing about bindings to `Group: dev` or `Group: qa`, so she keeps any access granted to those groups. To cut access you must find every binding that matches her username or any of her groups (`kubectl auth can-i --as=jane --as-group=dev …` helps), and remember that the certificate itself can't be revoked by Kubernetes.

stem: A user may `create` Roles and RoleBindings in namespace `team`, and otherwise can only `get` Pods there. They try to create a Role that grants `get` on Secrets. What happens?

options.text: It succeeds, because permission to create Roles is enough to define any rules at all
options.why: RBAC checks that the creator already holds the permissions in the rules.

options.text: Forbidden, unless they hold `get secrets` or `escalate` on roles
options.why: Privilege-escalation prevention stops you granting permissions you lack.

options.text: It succeeds, but the rule is stripped from the saved Role
options.why: The request is rejected outright rather than silently changed.

options.text: It succeeds only when the Role is bound to a ServiceAccount
options.why: The check happens when the Role is created, before any binding.

explanation: RBAC prevents privilege escalation: you can only create or update a Role whose permissions you already have (in the same scope), unless you hold the `escalate` verb on roles. Likewise, creating a binding to a Role requires holding its permissions or the `bind` verb.
reference: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization (Privilege escalation prevention)

stem: You need to change an existing RoleBinding so that it references the `view` ClusterRole instead of `edit`. What must you do?

options.text: Run `kubectl edit` and change `roleRef.name` from `edit` to `view`
options.why: The API server rejects updates to roleRef.

options.text: Delete the RoleBinding and create a new one with the new roleRef
options.why: `roleRef` is immutable once a binding is created.

options.text: Patch the `edit` ClusterRole so it matches `view`
options.why: That would change permissions for every other binding to `edit`.

options.text: Add a second roleRef entry; the most restrictive one wins
options.why: A binding has exactly one roleRef, and RBAC has no "most restrictive" logic.

explanation: A binding's `roleRef` is immutable. To point it at another role you delete and recreate the binding; `kubectl auth reconcile` can do this for you. The immutability prevents someone who can only update bindings from quietly swapping in a more powerful role for existing subjects.
